label: provisional
paradigm: These criteria serve a buyer choosing what to purchase, new or pre-owned: an evidence-based, value-aware buyer who wants an informed view of history and context. They are one reasonable buyer's stance, not the only one, and this version is provisional: drafted from published sources, not yet compiled or ratified.

change_log.reason: Drafted from WatchTime's chronograph buying guide, webChronos on column wheels versus cams, Time+Tide on servicing costs, Gear Patrol on fit, and the Teddy content audit of 2026-11-14.

spec_fields.complications: list of lower-case strings, for example "date", "chronograph", "gmt"; [] for time only

wearer.statement: What the buyer will time (short events, hours-long events, timing underwater, nothing) decides which chronograph features matter; most chronographs cannot be operated under water and many cannot time hours-long events.
The watch fits the buyer's wrist: lug-to-lug length inside the flat top of the wrist and a thickness the buyer's cuffs and comfort allow. Measure these rather than trusting the stated diameter.
wearer.test: Compare the stated lug-to-lug length with the buyer's measured flat wrist width; try the watch on where possible.

watch.statement: The watch has a chronograph (a stopwatch function).
Elapsed seconds, minutes and hours are easy to read: contrasting subdials and hands, a clear seconds track, not sacrificed to fashion.

An integrated chronograph movement rather than a module added to a time-only base: smoother push-piece feel and less amplitude drop when the chronograph runs (WatchTime measured 73.5 degrees for a modular and 19.5 for an integrated chronograph, in two watches).

Column wheel or cam switching. The evidence says performance is now equal; cams are cheaper, easier to adjust and service. A column wheel is chosen for push-piece feel, finishing and tradition, which is taste.
A vertical clutch, so the chronograph seconds hand starts without a jump and the chronograph can run continuously without excessive wear (useful as a running seconds hand).
The chronograph resolves the fractions the buyer needs: the finest step follows the movement frequency (28,800 vph gives 1/8 s, 36,000 vph 1/10 s), though the dial is often geared coarser.
Service cost and access. In-house chronographs tend to cost more and take longer to service; common third-party calibres are cheaper to service and parts are in ready supply.
